arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Grant argued the lower court misinterpreted the Westfall Act.
He claimed this interpretation unfairly deprives tort plaintiffs of basic procedural protections.
Justice Souter noted the government stated the employee acted within job scope.
Justice Ginsburg emphasized the employee was on premises claiming authority.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The Westfall Act transfers federal employee tort cases to federal court. It grants immunity if the employee acted within their job scope. The dispute centers on whether state courts can review that scope claim before transfer.

paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on October 30, 2006.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants state courts to review the employee's scope-of-employment claim before transferring the case.
the opposing side wants federal courts to decide the immunity question first, blocking state court review.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues the lower court misread the Westfall Act, stripping plaintiffs of basic procedural protections.
the opposing side argues federal law controls the immunity threshold, requiring federal court jurisdiction before state law applies.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Souter asked if the government's statement about job scope defines the immunity defense.
Justice Ginsburg asked why the claim is state law if federal immunity is the threshold issue.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case determines whether state courts can examine federal employee conduct claims. It affects access to state tort remedies for injured parties. It shapes the balance between federal immunity and state judicial power.
